food.text: Nomadic peoples of the Eurasian steppe had simple subsistence diets built primarily around dairy products, with game and plant foods playing a smaller role. Archaeobotanical evidence shows crop diffusion was already spreading across Central Asia's mountain valleys and oasis towns by the 3rd millennium BCE.

The Okunev culture of the Minusinsk Basin in south Siberia, dated from the end of the 3rd millennium BCE to the early 2nd millennium BCE, built its economy on raising cattle, sheep and goats, supplemented by hunting and fishing. Stone hoes, grain graters, pestles and a reaping sickle with a copper blade and horn handle show that farming was also part of their food supply.

The Andronovo culture spanned a vast area from the southern Urals to the upper Yenisei River and western Xinjiang between about 2000 and 1150 BCE, with sites reaching as far south as Tajikistan and Uzbekistan. Its earliest stage, beginning in the last years of the 3rd millennium BCE, focused on grazing cattle across the region's grasslands.

Within the Bactria–Margiana Archaeological Complex of southern Central Asia, which thrived between about 2500 and 1700 BCE, camels were domesticated. A model of a cart pulled by a camel, dated to around 2200 BCE, was found at the site of Altyn-Depe, showing the animal already being used to move goods.

At the Tasbas and Begash sites in the Kazakh highland steppe, archaeologists found the earliest evidence of nomadic herders using domesticated grains, dating to between 2800 and 2300 BCE. The wheat Triticum turgidum and the millet Panicum miliaceum found there mark the first known transmission of these crops from China and the lands south of the Syr Darya river into Central Eurasia.

The Krotov culture, active in the Altai steppe and forest-steppe of western Siberia from about 2000 to 1200 BCE, raised horses and cattle alongside equal numbers of sheep and goats, while still hunting and fishing. In summer these Altaians grazed their herds on alpine meadows, and in winter they returned to the river valleys, where they grew millet, barley, rye and other cereal grains.

Around 2000 BCE, contact between the Bactria–Margiana Archaeological Complex and the steppes to the north grew more intense. In the delta of the Amu Darya, people resembling Andronovo culture nomads began channelling river water for irrigation agriculture, a shift toward farming known as the Tazabagyab culture.

The Karakum Desert site of Adji Kui in Turkmenistan was occupied for about 1,100 years, from around 2400 to 1300 BCE. Archaeobotanical evidence shows crop diffusion was already spreading across the region's mountain valleys and oasis towns as early as the 3rd millennium BCE.

The Okunev people of the Minusinsk Basin used two- and four-wheeled carts, shown in rock art from the end of the 3rd millennium BCE. The design of these carts points to a connection with the western regions of Central Asia rather than Eastern Europe.

The earliest known domesticated grains used by nomadic herders (2800 to 2300 BC) were found at Tasbas and Begash on the Kazakh highland steppe. Triticum turgidum and panicum miliaceum there represent the first known transmission of these grains from China and the region south of the Syr Darya into Central Eurasia.

art.text: The most striking artifacts of ancient Mongolian sculpture are deer stones, Bronze Age megaliths that depicted deer in an ornamented setting. About 500 of them, making up 80% of all those known across the vast Eurasian steppe zone, are concentrated in the north and northwest of Mongolia.

Deer stones are ancient megaliths carved with symbols, found across central and eastern Eurasia but concentrated in Siberia and Mongolia. Of about 900 found in Central Asia and Siberia, around 700 are in Mongolia. Most stand near ancient graves, and it is believed the stones were guardians of the dead.

The prehistoric animal style art of the pastoral nomads of Central Asian grasslands, from the late second millennium BC, shows their zoomorphic mythologies and shamanic traditions. It also shows how easily they worked the symbols of settled societies into their own artworks.
Bronze Age craftsmen working in the Scytho-Siberian style decorated knife handles with the heads of a deer, ram or goat. The animals were shown with enlarged ears, protruding eyes and spiral horns.

Scholars disagree about where deer stone art came from. H. L. Chlyenova traced the deer image to the Saka tribe, and Volkov linked its crafting methods to the Scythians. D. Tseveendorj argued it began in Mongolia in the Bronze Age and then spread to Tuva and the Baikal area.

Some deer stones carry carved human faces of a Europoid type, with long faces, long noses, and deeply carved, close-set eyes. Other figures on these stones appear hooded, in a style linked to the Early Nomadic or Scytho-Siberian tradition.

The neighboring Okunev culture was active in the Minusinsk Basin from about 2550 to 1900 BCE. It developed an even more elaborate tradition of anthropomorphic stelae than the Chemurchek culture to its south.

Many BMAC strongholds continued to be occupied after steppe influence grew. Coarse incised pottery of the Tazabagyab-Andronovo culture turns up inside them, alongside earlier BMAC pottery, and also in pastoral camps outside their mudbrick walls.
The Karasuk culture, known for its decorated knife handles, originated in Mongolia. From there it spread northwards to Siberia and southwards to Yin China, carrying its metalworking style with it.

Known deer stones are unevenly spread. Mongolia has 550, the Lake Baikal area 20, the Sayan Altai 20 and the Altai Mountain regions 60. Later inhabitants likely reused the stones to mark their own burial mounds.

After about 1900 BC, each oasis of the Bactria–Margiana civilisation developed its own types of pottery and other objects. Coarse incised pottery from the Tazabagyab-Andronovo culture to the north also turned up inside BMAC strongholds, alongside the earlier BMAC pottery.

The oldest deer stones are the simpler Saian-Altai and Mongolian designs, dated to about 1300 BCE. Because their designs show no clear artistic evolution, researchers think the tradition may first have developed on a perishable material such as wood before being carved in stone.

At Yagshiin khuduu in Bulgan soum, Khovd aimag, archaeologists found what has been called the oldest kurgan stelae discovered in Mongolia. The site belongs to the Chemurchek culture and is dated to about 2500 to 2000 BCE.

The earliest style of deer stone, known as the Classical Mongolian type, appears to have developed first. This suggests an even older, pre-deer-stone tradition before 1500 BCE that originated in the northern Siberian taiga forest.

war.text: The horse-drawn chariot appears on the steppe in the 3rd millennium BC. By 2000 BC it took the form of war chariots with spoked wheels, which were more maneuverable and dominated the battlefields.
The Bronze Age BMAC civilisation had sustained contact with the Eurasian steppes to the north, intensifying c. 2000 BC. About 1900 BC its walled centres decreased sharply in size.

The earliest known chariots have been found in Sintashta burials in the Southern Urals. The culture is considered a strong candidate for the origin of the technology, which spread across the Old World and played an important role in ancient warfare.

The Sintashta culture was marked by high levels of militarism and extensive fortified settlements, of which 23 are known. Endemic intertribal warfare, already present in the earlier Abashevo culture, was intensified in the Sintashta period by ecological stress and competition for resources. This drove the building of fortifications on an unprecedented scale and the invention of the war chariot. Rival groups may also explain the extravagant sacrifices seen in Sintashta burials, as they sought to outdo one another in conspicuous consumption.

Seima-Turbino burial sites are spread across northern Eurasia and hold similar bronze weapons. The people buried there were nomadic warriors and metal-workers, travelling on horseback or on two-wheeled carts. Their homeland is considered to be the Altai Mountains.

Arkaim is a fortified site in the steppe of the Southern Urals, belonging to the Sintashta culture. More than twenty other structures built to similar patterns have been found from the southern Urals to northern Kazakhstan, forming the so-called "Land of Towns".

Archaeological evidence suggests Abashevo society was intensely warlike. Mass graves reveal inter-tribal battles involving hundreds of warriors on both sides, and a well-known kurgan at Pepkino held the remains of twenty-eight males who appear to have died violent deaths. Warfare appears to have been more frequent in the late Abashevo period, and it was in this turbulent environment that the Sintashta culture emerged. High-status graves contained weapons along with silver and copper ornaments.

Around 2000 BC the always precarious irrigation systems that had supported extensive agriculture failed. Together with the growing use of the horse, this gave rise to pastoral nomadism, which dominated the region by 1000 BC and led to the Scythian expansion.

Late Shang artifacts from Anyang, such as socketed spearheads with a single side hook, resemble Seima-Turbino ones. They were made precisely at the same time the Shang reported intense, protracted conflicts with the northern "Guifang" ("Devil's Country") tribes. This suggests the Guifang were the Seima-Turbino culture itself, and that their century-long conflict with the Shang led to the transfer of objects and manufacturing techniques.

Seima-Turbino weapons were made of tin bronze whose ore came from the Sayan and Altai Mountains region. Later finds point more specifically to the southeastern Altai and Xinjiang as the origin of the culture.

The Krotov culture of the Altai area developed entirely new designs of socketed weapons. Its metalworking tribes formed one component of the Seima-Turbino Phenomenon, and they then migrated rapidly to Western Siberia, the Urals and Eastern Europe.

Sintashta spoke-wheeled chariots were buried together with horses in Sintashta kurgans around 2000 to 1800 BC. The spread of these horses across Asia in the early-to-mid second millennium BC coincided with the spread of chariotry.

The socketed spearhead with a single side hook seems to go back to the Taosi culture, around 2100 to 2000 BCE, when the earliest Seima-Turbino types appear in China. This suggests Chinese bronze metallurgy first derived from the cultures of the Eurasian steppes.

Anthony and Vinogradov dated a chariot burial at Krivoye Lake to around 2000 BC. This answers scholars who thought Andronovo was too late to be Indo-Iranian, since chariot-using Aryans appear in Mitanni by the 15th century BC.

literature.text: Proto-Indo-Iranian is the reconstructed ancestor language of the Indo-Iranian branch, and its speakers are often connected with the Sintashta culture of the Eurasian Steppe in the late 3rd millennium BCE. It was likely removed by less than a millennium from its descendants Vedic Sanskrit, the language of the Rigveda, and Old Avestan, the language of the Gathas.

The Andronovo culture, a group of related Late Bronze Age cultures, spanned from the southern Urals to the upper Yenisei River in central Siberia and reached as far as western Xinjiang, flourishing from about 2000 to 1150 BC. Scholars broadly agree that the people of this vast steppe culture spoke an Indo-Iranian language.

The Gathas are the central hymns of Zoroastrianism, traditionally attributed to Zarathustra himself and composed in the oldest attested Iranian language. While Zoroastrian tradition dates Zarathustra to the 6th century BCE, many scholars now favor a much earlier date, with some placing the Gathas as early as 1500 BCE.

The Avesta, the collection of Zoroastrian scripture, was originally composed entirely as oral texts, with composition possibly beginning as early as the 15th century BCE. Its written transmission did not start until many centuries later, with the creation of a special Avestan alphabet.

Turya, or the Turanians, is the name in the Avesta for a people who closely interacted with the early Iranians, called the Aryas. Their true identity is unknown, but they are assumed to have been Iranic horse nomads from the Eurasian steppe, and their name lives on in the later toponym Turan.

Proto-Indo-Iranian is thought to have had a pitch-accent system much like that of modern Japanese, marked in reconstructions by an acute accent over the stressed vowel. This trait, inherited from Proto-Indo-European, also shaped Vedic Sanskrit and Avestan, even though Avestan itself was never written down.
Scholars connect this archaic language and imagery to Iranian tribes moving into Southern Central Asia, a migration occurring sometime in the mid to late 2nd millennium BCE.

In the Ushtavaiti Gatha, verse Y. 46.12 names Friia, a member of the Turya family, as a follower of Asha and Ahura Mazda. This suggests that in the earliest layer of Zoroastrian scripture, the steppe-dwelling Turanians could be viewed favorably, unlike their hostile role in later texts.

The word 'Gatha,' meaning song or hymn, is cognate with the Sanskrit word 'gatha,' and both trace back to a reconstructed Proto-Indo-Iranian word for 'song,' itself derived from a root meaning 'to sing.'

The Danus are another group named in the Avesta, either a clan of the Turyas or otherwise closely associated with them. In Yt. 13.37–38 the Fravashis are presented as helping the Aryas in their fight against the Turyan Danus. Their name has been connected to the Iranian word for river and to the mythical Danava race of the Vedas, though their exact identity is unknown.

Yasht 13.143, part of the Frawardin Yasht venerating the Fravashis, is specifically dedicated to venerating all the faithful people living in the lands of both the Aryas and the Turyas. This detail shows the steppe frontier between Iranians and Turanians was imagined as home to a shared spiritual community.

science.text: Tin is essential for making bronze, and it had to travel long distances. Archaeometallurgical studies show that trade in tin neither stopped nor decreased after 1200 BC, even though the closest sources of the metal were the modern regions of Afghanistan, Kazakhstan, or perhaps even Cornwall, England.

Recent evidence suggests that an early and now-extinct strain of the bubonic plague was brought from central Asia by the Sea Peoples or other migrating groups. It may have precipitated or worsened the collapse of cultures in Mycenaean Greece, Hittite Anatolia, and the Levant.

The Seima-Turbino culture is a pattern of burial sites with similar bronze artifacts, found across northern Eurasia, particularly Siberia and Central Asia. Its people are thought to have possessed advanced metal working technology. Recent studies date the complex to about 2200–1900 BCE, and its homeland is considered to be the Altai Mountains.

A genomic study published in 2021 examined the early Bronze Age Tarim mummies, dating from 2,135 to 1,623 BCE. They had about 72% Ancient North Eurasian ancestry and about 28% from Ancient Northeast Asians, particularly the Baikal_EBA, with no detectable Western Steppe Herder-related ancestry.

Indo-Iranian groups of Central Asia formed through admixture between local BMAC and Andronovo-related populations. This happened near the end of the Bronze Age and the early Iron Age, coinciding with the end of the Oxus Civilization.

In the Baikal region, the proportion of Ancient North Eurasian-related ancestry rose significantly over time. It climbed from a minimum of 14.3% in the Early Neolithic population to 22.7% in Late Neolithic and Bronze Age populations.

Models of two-wheeled carts from c. 3000 BC found at Altyn-Depe are the earliest evidence of wheeled transport in Central Asia. A model of a cart drawn by a camel, dated to c. 2200 BC, was also found there.

The Zhukaigou culture (2200–1500 BCE) in the Ordos Desert was home to early Xianbei. Their maternal DNA corresponds to that of the Mongol Daur people and the Tungusic Evenks. The Zhukaigou Xianbei also had trade relations with the Shang.

An analysis of Scytho-Siberian maternal DNA lineages from the Altai region found that, prior to the Iron Age, all ancient maternal lineages there were of West Eurasian origin. Iron Age specimens showed West Eurasian lineages reduced by 50% and East Asian lineages increased by 50%.

The Early Bronze Age Baikal populations, associated with the Glazkovo culture, date to circa 2500 BCE. They cluster broadly with other Ancient Northeast Asian groups but appear slightly differentiated, due to genetic drift associated with an earlier inland expansion route.

Modern Yaghnobis can be used as proxies for the pre-Iron Age Indo-Iranian substrate of Central Asia. They did, however, receive some Baikal Hunter-Gatherer ancestry that was absent in pre-Iron Age Central Asians.

In southern Bactrian sites like Sappali Tepe, links with the Andronovo culture increased over time. During the period 1700 to 1500 BCE, metal artefacts from Sappali Tepe derive from the Tazabagyab-Andronovo culture.

politics.text: The Sintashta culture, which flourished in the Southern Urals around 2200 to 1900 BCE, was marked by high levels of militarism. Endemic intertribal warfare, already present in the earlier Abashevo culture, was intensified by ecological stress and competition for resources. This drove fortification on an unprecedented scale, and at least 23 fortified settlements have been identified. Many Sintashta graves are furnished with weapons, and the burials show extravagant sacrifices that may reflect rivals trying to outdo one another.

The Bactria-Margiana Archaeological Complex, also called the Oxus civilization, was a Bronze Age civilization of Central Asia dated to about 2200 to 1700 BC. It was centered on the upper Amu Darya river, in what are now Turkmenistan, Afghanistan, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan.

The Seima-Turbino phenomenon linked nomadic warrior-metalworkers across a vast stretch of Siberia and Central Asia, from the Altai Mountains to Mongolia, China, Korea and Japan. These people traveled on horseback or two-wheeled carts and were buried with advanced bronze weapons.

The Sintashta culture also produced the earliest known chariots, found in its burials. The article says the war chariot was invented as endemic intertribal warfare, intensified by competition for resources, drove innovation in military technique. The technology spread throughout the Old World and played an important role in ancient warfare. Higher-status Sintashta graves held chariots alongside axes, mace-heads and spearheads.

Already in the Bronze Age, during the 3rd and 2nd millennia BC, growing settlements in Central Asia were part of an extensive trade network. This network linked the region to the Indus Valley, Mesopotamia and Egypt.

The Karasuk culture spread across Central Asia and southern Siberia from about 1500 BC onward. It used horse-drawn spoke-wheeled chariots whose design closely resembled chariots used by China's Shang dynasty around 1200 BC.

Some Shang dynasty bronze artifacts from the tomb of Fu Hao, who died around 1200 BCE, closely resemble Seima-Turbino weapons. This has led some researchers to suggest the Seima-Turbino people may have been the Guifang, a northern people the Shang fought for a century.

Karasuk bronze styles were copied throughout Central and Eastern Asia. The royal complex of the Anyang Cemetery, from the Shang dynasty period, contains numerous bronze objects imitating the Karasuk model.

culture.text: The Andronovo culture was a collection of similar local Late Bronze Age cultures that flourished c. 2000–1150 BC. It spread from the southern Urals to the upper Yenisei River in central Siberia and western Xinjiang, and in the south it reached Tajikistan and Uzbekistan.

The Bactria–Margiana Archaeological Complex, also known as the Oxus Civilization, was a Middle Bronze Age civilisation of southern Central Asia. It thrived between about 2500 BCE and 1700 BCE, though scholars debate the details.

Bronze Age Mongolia, from about 3000 to 700 BCE, saw a shared pastoral tradition of building monumental stone burial mounds and standing stones. This tradition began with the Afanasievo culture and continued through the Okunev and Chemurchek cultures.

The Chemurchek culture of western Mongolia and Xinjiang, dated about 2750 to 1900 BCE, buried its dead in large rectangular stone-fenced tombs built around collective burials. The bodies lay supine with flexed legs, a position similar to that of the Afanasievo culture. Beside the tombs, on their eastern side, stood anthropomorphic stones with flattened faces, straight noses and globular eyes. The figures appear naked, since pectoral muscles seem to be depicted.
The Siberian Okunev culture is dated to about 2700 to 1800 BCE. It kept a long tradition of totemic standing stones going back to the third millennium BCE.

The Afanasievo culture of south Siberia, dated c. 3300 to 2500 BCE, is named after Gora Afanasieva in Khakassia. Its burials have been found as far as Shatar Chuluu in central Mongolia, about 1,500 km beyond the Altai Mountains.

Anthony & Vinogradov (1995) dated a chariot burial at Krivoye Lake to around 2000 BC. Kuzmina (1994) argues that the chariot supports identifying the Andronovo culture as Indo-Iranian, since Indo-Aryans used it in Mitanni and Vedic India.

The Andronovo culture moved intensively eastwards through the 2nd millennium BC, in the Alakul Phase (2000–1700 BC) and the Fedorovo Phase (1850–1450 BC). It expanded as far as the Upper Yenisei River, succeeding the non-Indo-European Okunev culture.
The Afanasievo culture is named after a nearby mountain, Gora Afanasieva, in Bogradsky District, Khakassia, Russia. The archaeologist Sergei Teploukhov first excavated it from 1920 to 1929.

Afanasievo burials were single or small collective graves, with the dead usually laid flexed on their back in a pit, and the pits were arranged in rectangular, sometimes circular, enclosures marked by stone walls. Mass graves were not usual, but at Afanasevo Gora one grave held seven people, and two strains of Yersinia pestis, the plague bacterium, were extracted from their teeth, dated 2909–2679 BCE and 2887–2677 BCE. The strain's genes express flagellin, which triggers the human immune response, so it was not a bubonic plague. It has been argued that the enclosures represent family burial plots, with four or five enclosures making up the local social group.

The Seima-Turbino culture is dated to about 2200 to 1900 BCE and is known from burial sites with similar bronze artifacts. Its buried people were nomadic warriors and metal-workers on horseback or two-wheeled carts, and the culture is attested perhaps as far as Korea and Japan.

According to David W. Anthony, the Afanasievo people descended from migrants who crossed the Eurasian Steppe c. 3700–3300 BCE from the Repin culture of the Don-Volga region. Their genomes were very close to those of the Yamnaya population of the Pontic–Caspian steppe.

In the delta of the Amu Darya, people whose remains resemble those of Andronovo nomads channelled the river's waters for irrigation agriculture. This is interpreted as nomads settling down to farming after contact with the BMAC, and it is known as the Tazabagyab culture.

About 1900 BC the walled BMAC centres decreased sharply in size. Tazabagyab-Andronovo coarse incised pottery appears inside many BMAC strongholds, alongside the earlier BMAC pottery, and also in pastoral camps outside the mudbrick walls.
Petroglyphs of animals are associated with the area and period of the Afanasievo culture. They share similarities with petroglyphs found in western and central Asia.
In the highlands above the Bactrian oases in Tajikistan, kurgan cemeteries of the Vaksh and Bishkent type appeared. Their pottery mixed elements of the late BMAC and Tazabagyab-Andronovo traditions.
